title: Adjectives: describing people and things
goal: Match adjectives to their nouns, describe people and places, and make simple comparisons.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nowy współlokator
dialogs.intro: A bench outside the dorm. Budi has been sharing a place with someone new for a week.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: So what's your new roommate like?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Nice and calm. A bit shy.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Wysoki, ciemne włosy, okulary. Wygląda poważnie, ale jest zabawny.
lines.id: Tall, dark hair, glasses. He looks serious, but he's funny.
lines.literal: tall, dark hair, glasses. looks seriously, but is funny.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Chyba dwadzieścia pięć. Jest z Wietnamu.
lines.id: Twenty-five, I think. He's from Vietnam.
lines.literal: probably twenty five. is from Vietnam.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.id: And your apartment? Is it big?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nie bardzo. Małe, ale jasne i czyste. Kuchnia jest nowa.
lines.id: Not really. Small, but bright and clean. The kitchen is new.
lines.literal: not very. small, but bright and clean. kitchen is new.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: To najważniejsze. Moje mieszkanie jest tanie, ale ciemne i zimne.
lines.id: That's what matters most. Mine is cheap, but dark and cold.
lines.literal: that most-important. my apartment is cheap, but dark and cold.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Stary budynek. Zimą muszę nosić sweter w domu.
lines.id: It's an old building. In winter I have to wear a sweater indoors.
lines.literal: old building. in-winter I-must wear sweater in home.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Współczuję. Może przenieś się bliżej centrum?
lines.id: I'm sorry. Maybe move closer to the center?
lines.literal: I-sympathize. maybe move self closer center?

notes: **Jaki? Jaka? Jakie?** — even the question word "what kind of" follows the noun's gender. *Jaki jest twój pokój?* (m), *Jaka jest twoja siostra?* (f), *Jakie jest twoje mieszkanie?* (n).
**Ciemne włosy** — plural. Hair in Polish is always plural, like "hairs", and the adjective is plural too. The same goes for *okulary* (glasses) and *drzwi* (door), which have no singular form.

**Wygląda poważnie** — "he looks serious". After *wyglądać* you use the adverb (*poważnie*), not the adjective (*poważny*). Compare *jest poważny* (he is serious) with *wygląda poważnie* (he looks serious).
**Małe, jasne, czyste** — all end in *-e* because they describe *mieszkanie*, a neuter word. Notice that every adjective in the row changes, not just the first.
**Najważniejsze** — the "most" form: the prefix *naj-* goes on the comparative form. *Ważny → ważniejszy → najważniejszy*. The pattern is the same for almost all adjectives.

**Niedobrze** — the prefix *nie-* is written as one word with adverbs and adjectives: *dobry → niedobry*, *drogi → niedrogi*, *daleko → niedaleko*. Notice the difference from *nie* standing alone before a verb.
**Zimą** — winter as a time expression, the form you know from unit 11. Compare *zima jest długa* (the winter is long) with *zimą jest zimno* (in winter it's cold).
**Współczuję** — "I sympathize", an everyday expression of sympathy, much lighter than "my condolences". For real bad news people say *moje kondolencje*.

grammars.title: Adjective endings
body: An adjective always adapts to the noun it describes — in gender, number and form.
after: The **-i** ending is used when the stem ends in *k*, *g* or a soft letter: *polski*, *drogi*, *tani*. Otherwise it's **-y**: *dobry*, *nowy*, *stary*.
Adjectives also change when their noun changes form: *dobra kawa* → *dobrą kawę* (object) → *dobrej kawy* (negated). For now you only need the basic forms; the rest will come through habit.

The last row is the plural for groups that include men — a pattern you've already met in *ci*, *wszyscy*, *moi*. It often changes the last letter of the stem (*dobry → dobrzy*, *miły → mili*), and at A1 it's enough to recognize it.

grammars.title: Comparing
body: Two ways — and the second works for any adjective if you forget the first.
after: The four rows in bold are irregular — and they're the most common ones, just like English good/better/best. Learn all four now; you can form the rest yourself.

The last row shows the way out: long adjectives put ***bardziej*** (more) and ***najbardziej*** (most) in front, without changing the adjective at all — just like English "more interesting". When in doubt, this always works and is always correct.
"Than" in comparisons: ***niż*** or ***od***. *Kraków jest mniejszy niż Warszawa* — Kraków is smaller than Warsaw.

blocks.title: Describing someone in four sentences
items: *To jest mój kolega Adam.* — This is my friend Adam.
*Jest wysoki i ma ciemne włosy.* — He's tall and has dark hair.
*Ma dwadzieścia pięć lat i studiuje medycynę.* — He's twenty-five and studies medicine.
*Jest bardzo miły, ale trochę nieśmiały.* — He's very nice, but a bit shy.
These four sentences are a frame you can use for anyone. Just swap in the details.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Wolny* has two meanings, both common: **slow** (*wolny internet*) and **free / available** (*wolny stolik*). The context decides, and mixing them up rarely causes real trouble.

blocks.title: Giving your opinion politely
items: *Bardzo mi się podoba.* — I really like it. (for things, places, looks)
*Najlepsze, co jest.* — The best there is.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right adjective ending.

items: He's tall and has dark hair.
My room is small but bright.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: dobry — dobra — dobre — nowe — mały — tani
lepszy / najlepszy — większy / największy — mniejszy / najmniejszy — tańszy / najtańszy — gorszy / najgorszy
